stem: During X-ray production, an incoming high-speed electron passes close to a tungsten nucleus and is rapidly slowed and deflected. What is emitted as a result of this interaction?
justification: The text describes this exact collision: 'the incoming electron passes close to the tungsten nucleus and is rapidly slowed down and deflected with the emission of X-ray photons,' which is the mechanism producing the continuous spectrum.
source_book: Essentials of Dental Radiography and Radiology

stem: Below what tube voltage will characteristic K-line photons NOT be produced by a dental X-ray tube with a tungsten target?
justification: The chunk states 'Characteristic K-line photons are not produced by X-ray tubes with tungsten targets operating at less than 69.5 kV – referred to as the critical voltage,' directly identifying 69.5 kV as the threshold.
source_book: Essentials of Dental Radiography and Radiology

stem: According to the inverse square law described for X-ray physics, what happens to beam intensity when the distance from the X-ray source is doubled?
options: Intensity is reduced to one quarter
justification: The text explains that 'in free space, X-rays obey the inverse square law: doubling the distance from an X-ray source reduces the intensity to 1/4,' calling this a very important radiation protection principle.
source_book: Essentials of Dental Radiography and Radiology

stem: In manual chemical processing of a dental radiographic film, roughly how long should the film remain in the fixer solution?
justification: The processing steps state 'the film is immersed in fixer for about 8-10 minutes,' followed by washing and drying, giving the correct fixation time.
source_book: Essentials of Dental Radiography and Radiology

stem: In the developer solution used for manual film processing, which constituent acts as the restrainer that prevents fog and controls the activity of the developing agents?
justification: The table of developer constituents lists 'Benzotriazole - Restrainer - prevents fog and controls the activity of the developing agents,' identifying its specific function.
source_book: Essentials of Dental Radiography and Radiology

stem: What is a recognized disadvantage of using rapid/instant film processing chemicals compared with conventional processing?
options: It takes far longer than manual processing
Image quality is usually inferior to conventionally processed film
It cannot be used at all for intraoral films
It eliminates the need for a darkroom entirely
justification: The disadvantages listed include that 'image quality is usually inferior to conventional film processed manually or automatically' along with deterioration over time and lack of lead foil.
source_book: Essentials of Dental Radiography and Radiology

stem: On a digital radiographic image, what visual effect results from allocating every pixel the highest available numerical value?
options: Contrast is maximized with no grey tones
justification: The text explains that with brightness, 'taken to the extreme, every pixel would be allocated the highest number and the image would be totally white,' describing this specific effect on image appearance.
source_book: Essentials of Dental Radiography and Radiology

stem: A 68-year-old man reports sudden numbness of the lower right lip, with normal sensation preserved under the chin. Which nerve territory does this pattern of numbness most strongly implicate as being affected between the mandibular foramen and mental foramen?
justification: The case explains that 'the normal sensation under the chin is significant' because the nerve to mylohyoid supplies that area, so 'the cause must lie between the start of the inferior dental canal' and the mental foramen, implicating the inferior alveolar nerve.
source_book: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving in Dentistry

stem: In a patient presenting with jaw numbness and a destructive 'moth-eaten' radiolucency, breast and prostate metastases are unusual among jaw metastases because they sometimes cause what unexpected radiographic finding?
options: A large soft tissue mass with no bone change
Bone formation producing a sclerotic or mixed radiolucency
Complete absence of any radiographic change
Widening of the periodontal ligament space only
justification: The text notes 'breast and prostate metastases are unusual in that they sometimes cause bone formation at the site, producing a sclerotic or mixed radiolucency rather than the more typical pure moth-eaten poorly defined radiolucency.'
source_book: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving in Dentistry

stem: A patient develops an oroantral fistula after extraction of an upper first molar. According to the definition given, how long must the communication persist before it is classed as a fistula rather than a communication?
justification: The text defines an oroantral fistula as 'a persistent epithelialized communication between the maxillary antrum and the mouth, present for more than 48 hours,' distinguishing it from an unepithelialized communication.
source_book: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving in Dentistry

stem: At the time of an upper molar extraction, which clinical sign at the socket suggests an oroantral communication has occurred?
options: A dull, muffled sound on percussion of the adjacent tooth
An echoing 'wind tunnel sound' when a suction tip is held in the socket
Bleeding that stops immediately after extraction
Increased mobility of the neighboring tooth only
justification: The text states that if a communication is present, 'an echoing wind tunnel sound will be heard if a small suction tip is held in the socket, the result of air being sucked from the antrum as well as the mouth.'
source_book: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving in Dentistry

stem: A 38-year-old woman has recurrent mouth ulcers, usually one at a time, that have recently increased to 3-4 ulcers with greater frequency. Based on the classic presentation described, what is the most likely diagnosis?
justification: The case states 'the history is suggestive of RAS minor, which has recently increased in severity,' and the ulcer's irregular but well-defined margin with a halo of erythema is described as typical of this diagnosis.
source_book: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving in Dentistry

stem: A 55-year-old man has a painless, slowly enlarging neck lump found to be a cystic squamous cell carcinoma metastasis. Current guidelines recommend testing the tissue for which viruses when no primary tumor site is known?
options: High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)
Herpes simplex virus and varicella zoster
justification: The text states that once squamous differentiation is confirmed, 'current guidelines recommend testing the tissue for high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) if no primary is known,' since these viruses cause many oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal cancers.
source_book: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving in Dentistry

stem: During history-taking, when should sensibility (vitality) testing and percussion be performed on a recently traumatically displaced upper central incisor?
options: They should not be tested for loss of vitality or percussed at this early stage
Only after root canal treatment is complete
Sensibility testing should be repeated hourly on the day of injury
justification: The case explicitly states 'the teeth should not be percussed and should not be tested for loss of vitality at this stage. Sensibility tests have been shown to give false-negative results' shortly after luxation injuries.
source_book: Odell's Clinical Problem Solving in Dentistry

stem: When taking a presenting complaint history, why should a dentist avoid the introductory question 'What brought you here today?'
options: It is too formal and clinical for most patients
It gives the patient a chance to complain about transport or car parking rather than their dental problem
It cannot legally be asked without written consent
It confuses patients whose first language is not English
justification: The Oxford Handbook advises: 'Avoid "What brought you here today?" unless you want to give them the chance to complain about transport or car parking,' explaining the reasoning behind this recommendation.

stem: During a dental history, asking a patient 'How often do you brush your teeth and how long for?' is primarily intended to give the clinician information about which two things?
justification: The text notes this question yields '(motivation and likely gingival condition)' as the clinical value of asking about brushing frequency and duration.

stem: For most dental out-patients, when is a full formal medical examination (beyond simply recording a medical history) indicated?
options: For every routine check-up regardless of treatment planned
Only for patients undergoing general anaesthesia or with a positive medical history undergoing extensive treatment under LA or sedation
Only for patients over 65 years old
Never; medical examination is outside a dentist's scope
justification: The text states 'simply recording a medical history should suffice to screen for any potential problems. The exceptions are patients who are to undergo general anaesthesia and anyone with a positive medical history undergoing extensive treatment under LA or sedation.'

stem: According to the Oxford Handbook of Clinical Dentistry, what is the key to examining the mouth efficiently in routine clinical practice?
options: Developing a systematic approach that becomes almost automatic
Memorising every rare disease presentation before starting
Always performing the full new-patient examination on every attendee
Referring all symptomless patients for specialist assessment
justification: The text explains that the key is to develop a systematic approach, which becomes almost automatic, so that the routine symptomless attendee can be examined in a briefer format rather than following an exhaustive textbook description every time.
